claims.text: In fcc-based multi-principal-element alloys, a three-dimensional twin network enabled by low or negative stacking-fault energy governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
CrCoNi is a single-phase fcc medium-entropy alloy with a very low or negative stacking-fault energy and a propensity to form a three-dimensional twin network during deformation.
The three-dimensional twin network in CrCoNi remains stable against detwinning as deformation continues.
A slight compositional modification can raise stacking-fault energy and thereby suppress twinning while leaving phase and grain size similar.
The relevant high-temperature deformation regime is approximately 600–1000 °C at strain rates typical of industrial processing.
Controlled atmosphere and irradiation pretreatment can simulate the relevant fusion plasma-facing environment for this comparison.
Twin boundaries impede dislocation motion and thus contribute to high strength and substantial strain hardening.
Twin-boundary interfaces provide multiple pathways for dislocation motion and permit significant plastic deformation.
The combination of dislocation barriers and additional glide pathways delays localized plastic instability.
The twin-network mechanism enhances plastic strain capacity and toughness at elevated temperatures.
At high temperature, the lower-stacking-fault-energy alloy will develop a higher twin density than the elevated-stacking-fault-energy variant.
At high temperature, the lower-stacking-fault-energy alloy will exhibit greater strain hardening and fracture toughness than the elevated-stacking-fault-energy variant.
Prior studies establish high yield strength, significant uniform elongation, and high fracture toughness for the low-stacking-fault-energy baseline under high-temperature deformation.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase fcc alloys at roughly 600–1000 °C when deformation is dominated by dislocation slip and twin-mediated plasticity.
Secondary phases or environmentally induced phase instability may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Initial microstructure, temperature, strain, and strain rate influence high-temperature plastic-flow response.
The quantitative strengthening contribution from deformation twinning remains uncertain.
The interaction between twin-mediated deformation and diffusion-controlled processes at high temperature remains uncertain.
It is not established that a slight compositional modification can change stacking-fault energy without changing other important microstructural features.

Failure to observe a statistically significant improvement in strain hardening and fracture toughness with lower stacking-fault energy and higher twin density would falsify the proposed primary-mediator hypothesis.
